title: Ombudsman decision DRN-5994630 — Assurant General Insurance Limited
text:
DRN-5994630

The complaint

Mr S has complained about the method of repair Assurant General Insurance Limited
wanted to use to repair his mobile phone under his mobile phone insurance policy, when he
claimed given his mobile phone had been damaged.

What happened
Mr S took out his mobile insurance via his bank’s plan, which he joined.

Mr S damaged his phone and made a claim to Assurant who accepted it and organised for
Mr S to deliver his phone in for repair. Once repaired, Assurant sent his phone back to Mr S
but its courier left it in a shop instead of delivering it back to Mr S’ home address which
caused Mr S some inconvenience.

On receiving his phone back, Mr S was upset that it wasn’t working properly and that
unbranded parts had been used in repairing his phone. So he complained.

Assurant agreed Mr S was put to some trouble and upset in getting his phone back given the
courier caused confusion in not delivering it to him. So it paid him £25 compensation.
Given Mr S said his phone wasn’t working properly, Assurant said given it provided a
warranty for the repairs, it would look at his phone again and see what was wrong or what
had gone wrong. Mr S didn’t think it was a warranty issue so didn’t want to give his phone
back to Assurant. This meant he didn’t have a working phone which was causing him
additional inconvenience.

As Mr S remained unhappy, he brought his complaint to us. The investigator was of the view
that Assurant had done enough in both compensating Mr S for the delivery confusion and
offering to look at Mr S’ phone under its repair warranty, in order to see what went wrong
with the repair. Therefore she didn’t think Assurant had to do anything more at this stage.

Mr S remained dissatisfied so his complaint has been passed to me to decide.

What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having done so, I’m not upholding this complaint. I do appreciate that Mr S will be very
disappointed so I’ll now explain why.

How this policy was provided to Mr S

First Mr S’s bank decided with Assurant to provide this mobile phone policy, so that means
Mr S’ bank sold this policy to Mr S under its plan which Mr S signed up to. It also means the
bank was responsible in ensuring Mr S had sight of the policy terms before he decided to

pay for his bank’s plan to include the fact unbranded parts might be used to repair his phone,
if Mr S made a claim.

If Mr S didn’t know what was covered under this policy then he should raise a complaint
against his bank, since it was their job to have informed him of what this policy covered. In
this decision since I can only write a decision against one business at a time under our rules,
I’m only considering what Assurant might have done wrong here only. If Mr S thinks his bank
did something wrong then he will have to make a separate complaint to his bank.

Policy terms

So Mr S’ bank and Assurant agreed the mobile phone insurance policy terms which would
be offered to Mr S and other customers of his bank. Those terms say the following:

‘If your mobile phone is damaged or breaks down, we will either repair or replace it. If
your mobile phone is lost or stolen, we will replace it.
…
If your claim is approved, we will either repair your mobile phone or send you a
replacement.
…
Repairs will be made using readily available parts, or we may provide
remanufactured products. These may contain parts that are of similar or equivalent
specification, and these may include unbranded parts. This policy is provided in
addition to any manufacturer’s warranty that applies to your mobile phone
(“applicable manufacturer’s warranty”). Nothing in this policy is intended to affect your
rights under the applicable manufacturer’s warranty or your statutory rights.’

This means the policy terms do allow unbranded parts to be used to repair any phone. This
is very common in the mobile phone insurance industry as most mobile phone insurers will
often use unbranded parts to repair phones. So I don’t find it unusual or significant.

I have no authority to tell any insurer how it must repair a phone or what parts it should use.
That is part of the insurers’ commercial discretion and is permitted by the regulations under
which they operate. And so by deciding to be part of his bank’s plan, Mr S would also be
deemed to have accepted that unbranded parts might be used to repair his phone if he
made a claim.

Therefore I consider that Assurant hasn’t done anything wrong in using unbranded parts to
repair Mr S’ phone.

What Assurant did when Mr S claimed

Assurant decided it could repair Mr S’ phone and arranged to see it and then it repaired it.
The fact that it used some unbranded parts is permitted by the policy terms  as I explained
above, so that shows me Assurant didn’t do anything wrong in using unbranded parts.
It’s clear from Mr S’ account of what happened that his phone wasn’t working when Assurant
finally delivered it back to him. So it’s clear to me something went wrong when Assurant
repaired Mr S’ phone. However I don’t consider Assurant did anything wrong in asking Mr S
to send his phone back in again, so it could see what went wrong with the repair of his
phone. That would be the only way that Assurant could also decide how to make things right
again for Mr S.

When Assurant repaired Mr S’ phone it provided a warranty on those repairs so it said it was
going to find out what went wrong under its repair warranty only. Mr S mentioned that this
wasn’t a manufacturer warranty repair issue. I agree, it isn’t. Assurant has simply said it

would look at the faults Mr S highlighted, under its own ‘repair warranty’ (not under any
manufacturer’s warranty), in its efforts to make things right again for Mr S.

So there is nothing fundamentally wrong with Assurant wanting to examine the phone again,
as it’s right and indeed fair that if Assurant did something wrong in its original repair of Mr S’
phone, then it needs the chance to find out what that was, along with repairing it again, or if
it’s then not repairable, then replacing the phone at that stage.

Because Assurant hasn’t been able to find out what went wrong in its repair of Mr S’ phone
as Mr S doesn’t want to return his phone to Assurant, I have no evidence at all before me
which shows the repair was substandard as Mr S says, or that the faults occurred directly
from its repair (although that seems very likely), or that the parts used which might have
been unbranded parts caused compatibility and usability issues as Mr S also says. And I
consider that until Assurant can examine Mr S’ phone again, there is no evidence to show
me that it now must replace Mr S’ phone either, as Mr S now says he wants it to do.

Therefore it remains that I consider Assurant is correct on needing to see Mr S’ phone again,
before it can decide whether its initial repair caused these problems, whether these further
issues are capable of being fixed or not now, or whether it now needs to replace Mr S’ phone
instead. So it remains for Mr S to decide if he wants to send his phone back into Assurant or
not. But until he does allow Assurant to physically see his phone again, it remains that
Assurant is unable to help Mr S further at this stage.

However on the basis Mr S hasn’t yet sent his phone back to Assurant, I also consequently
can’t hold Assurant responsible for Mr S not having a working phone since Assurant
returned his phone back to him. This is because Assurant hasn’t delayed in trying to sort out
the issue, the delay has happened because Mr S didn’t want to send his phone back to
Assurant to check to see what went wrong. Therefore Assurant is not responsible for the fact
Mr S remains without a properly working phone.

The confusion caused by the courier company in getting Mr S’ phone back to him after
Assurant repaired it

There is no dispute that the courier instructed by Assurant to deliver Mr S’ phone back to him
after it had been repaired didn’t notify Mr S it was delivering back his phone. And then the
courier service notified him it had been left in some shop. Assurant agreed this was below its
usual service standard and has paid Mr S £25 compensation.

So for that courier’s mistake and the consequent running around Mr S had to do to locate his
phone, I consider the amount of £25 compensation is adequate. This is in line with our
stated approach to compensation more fully detailed on our website. So I consider it’s fair
and reasonable here.

Conclusion

The policy provides that unbranded parts can be used in any mobile phone repair, therefore
it follows that Assurant hasn’t done anything wrong in using them.
The phone clearly wasn’t working properly when Mr S received his phone back from
Assurant, following its repair. However without Mr S permitting Assurant to find out what
went wrong and whether it’s further repairable, then Assurant can’t help Mr S further at this
stage. It’s not fair and reasonable for Assurant to provide Mr S with a replacement phone as
Mr S now wishes, unless it can see what went wrong with the original repair, first. So it
remains for Mr S to decide to send his phone back in, before Assurant can then do anything
further to make things right again.

Because Assurant had repaired this phone and given a warranty on those repairs,
Assurant’s offer to look at the phone again was being done under its own warranty, not any
manufacturer’s warranty as Mr S appears to believe.

Assurant did cause Mr S some inconvenience when its courier didn’t return the phone
directly to Mr S. So paying Mr S £25 compensation is also fair and reasonable.

My final decision
So, for these reasons, it’s my final decision that I don’t uphold this complaint.

Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr S to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Rona Doyle
Ombudsman
